subject: typewriter
pitch: A 1930s typewriter in glossy racing green. Round keys with cream letters on chrome rims in four staggered rows, a semicircle of thin type bars behind them, a chrome carriage return lever, a black platen roller with a sheet of paper half typed, and a small brass maker's badge on the front.
reasoning:
I'm planning a single TypeScript module for a typewriter prop, adding a root joint called "body" to satisfy the builder's requirement even though props don't strictly need articulation, and sketching rough dimensions around 0.36 wide, 0.38 deep, and 0.22 tall.

Working out the extruded side profile for the sloped keyboard deck and housing...

I'm finalizing the body outline avoiding self-crossing, then working out the four staggered key rows along the sloped keyboard surface, positioning each key as a chrome-rimmed cylinder with a cream disc top for the letter.

For the letters, I decide against one giant texture atlas and instead generate 26 small individual SVG textures (one per letter) placed as a plane on each key's sloped top. I lay out the standard QWERTY rows—10, 10, 9, and 7 keys—with 0.027 spacing fitting within the 0.36 width, and apply progressive stagger offsets to each row for realism.

Working out the key orientation and normal vectors for the sloped keyboard...

I'm layering the chrome rim cylinder and cream cap cylinder for each key, positioning the decal slightly above the cap surface along the normal direction so the letter sits visibly on top.

Now I'm placing the space bar as a chrome box floating above the lower keyboard face, positioning it near the front edge at a slightly raised height relative to the slope profile.

I'm also planning a small brass badge on the front face with a decorative text decal for a fictional brand name, plus adding a chrome trim strip along the front edge.

For the base, I'm deciding whether to add small black feet at the corners to keep the body clear of y=0, but I'll just shift the body profile upward slightly rather than complicate the math with offsets.

Now I'm working out the typebar basket behind the keys—thinking of it as a fan of thin bars radiating from a hinge semicircle up to a convergence point above the platen, placing the hinge circle in the XZ plane near the back-slope region.

Still planning typebar geometry...

I'm positioning the platen cylinder with knobs and support plates, then working out the paper sheet as a thin angled box that wraps from behind the platen up and over its top, simplifying the curve into a tilted flat shape.

Continuing the path coordinates up and over the platen, but I'm realizing real typewriters actually feed paper from behind, wrap it under the platen, and bring it up the front where the typed lines appear rising above the printing line—so I should reconsider the wrap direction to match that physical behavior.

Still plotting curve points...

I'm making the text plane transparent except where the letters appear, using a monospace font rendered in a small SVG, bold enough to survive alpha thinning, with paper color showing through behind it. Then I'm positioning the paper sweep relative to the platen so it hugs the roller radius without clipping into other parts.

I'm now working out the paper bail rod placement -- adjusting its position and radius so it rests just in front of the paper without intersecting it, while making sure it still passes cleanly through the side plates given their depth and offset.

Then I shift to designing the carriage return lever: a chrome rod curving outward and upward from the left plate's top-front edge, ending in a small ball-shaped chrome tip.

For the platen knobs, I'm placing black cylindrical knobs with chrome hubs at each end of the platen axis, and I'll add chrome-ish ribbon spool discs on top of the body.

I'm checking spool placement against the basket hinge bars and side plates to avoid geometry collisions, adjusting the x-position so the chrome spool disc with its black ribbon cylinder clears the plate's inner face.

I nudge the tip point to z -0.092, y 0.252 so it sits just in front of the paper path without colliding, checking that the bottom of the paper arc still clears the body top. I'm also considering adding a thin chrome trim strip along the lower front edge of the body for detail.

I'm skipping extra gloss and pinstripe details, and checking plate and key geometry fits within the ±0.18 body width. For color I'm using a dark green body with a slightly darker shade, and adding a rear crossbar box to connect the side plates near the carriage area.

Now I'm setting up the key layout logic: four rows (numbers, QWERTY, ASDF, ZXCV) positioned from back to front with a sloped y-offset per row for the typewriter's curved keyboard look, plus horizontal stagger offsets and x-spacing per key based on row length.

I'm generating per-letter key textures as small SVG circles with a serif letter in the center, then applying them as textures on tiny circle geometries for each key.

For the paper, I'm sweeping a flat box-shaped cross-section along a path in the YZ plane to form the curved paper strip, with a cream color. For the bars, I'm sweeping a bezier curve with a thin round cross-section and theme-based color.

I'm computing the bezier control points so each bar funnels from its hinge point outward toward a shared target point, with control points offset in y and angled using sine/cosine of theta to create a converging, cone-like shape.

I'm adding the hinge ring as a semicircular arc of points for the catmull curve, laying out 15 type bars spaced across a theta sweep from -70 to 70 degrees, and designing a brass badge decal plane with rounded-rect text reading "VERDANT" and "No. 7," plus a thin brass backing box to mount it on the front face.

Now I'm sketching the plane's text content as a typewritten letter excerpt ("Dear Sir, Pursuant to your letter...") rendered via SVG with monospace bold strokes across several lines, positioned to fill the lower half of the badge plane.

I'm reconsidering the plane's placement though—since the sheet is scrolled through a typewriter, the already-typed text should sit above the printing line with blank paper below it, so I need to center the plane higher with text filling from the top down, leaving the bottom portion blank.

Working out the exact plane position and orientation for the text overlay, with a small normal offset so it sits just above the paper surface without clipping into it.
